title: Influence of sequential isomaltulose vs. a maltodextrin:fructose mixture on substrate utilization during endurance cycling
summary:
During physical exertion, the body derives energy from both carbohydrates and fat, with the relative proportion depending mainly on exercise intensity. Especially in sports with varying intensity, such as road cycling, it is important to preserve the body's own carbohydrate stores (glycogen) so that a high-intensity effort, such as a final sprint, remains possible even after prolonged exertion. During training, readily available carbohydrates such as maltodextrin combined with fructose are commonly used; however, this can cause fluctuating blood glucose levels and may inhibit fat burning. Isomaltulose, by contrast, is a more slowly absorbed carbohydrate that may contribute to a more stable blood glucose course and, in turn, to more favorable fat oxidation.

The aim of this pilot study is to investigate, using indirect calorimetry (spiroergometry), how repeated intake of isomaltulose during a 90-minute, moderate-intensity endurance exercise bout on a cycle ergometer affects fat and carbohydrate metabolism compared with a classic maltodextrin-fructose mixture. In contrast to previous studies, participants first eat a standardized breakfast, and carbohydrate intake occurs repeatedly during exercise, in order to reflect a realistic training and competition scenario. Afterward, a short maximal sprint test, the so-called Wingate test, is additionally performed to assess anaerobic performance capacity.

A total of 20 healthy, endurance-trained road cyclists from the Munich/Upper Bavaria region are to take part in the study, 10 women and 10 men. Participants first undergo a sports-medical screening examination including a medical history, physical examination, resting ECG, and a specific strength test. This is followed by four testing sessions, each separated by at least three days. At the first session, a baseline assessment determines maximal oxygen uptake as well as the exercise intensity corresponding to the highest fat oxidation rate. At the second session, participants complete a 90-minute exercise bout during which only water is provided. At the two subsequent sessions, participants complete a 90-minute exercise bout during which either isomaltulose or the maltodextrin-fructose mixture is provided, each followed by the concluding sprint test. Throughout all exercise sessions, respiratory gases are continuously measured via spiroergometry, and blood glucose and lactate levels are measured from capillary blood taken from the earlobe.
conditions: The rate of fat oxidation versus carbohydrate metabolism during endurance exercise, under the influence of different substrates.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Age > 18 years
- Physical health, defined as an unremarkable medical history regarding cardiovascular, pulmonary, orthopedic, and metabolic diseases
- No limitations that would prevent completion of a maximal spiroergometry test
- Presence of written informed consent
- Regular endurance sport activity (road cycling)
- VO2max ≥ 55 ml/min/kg (male) or ≥ 50 ml/min/kg (female)
Exclusion criteria:
- Known cardiovascular, pulmonary, orthopedic, neurological, or metabolic diseases
- Pregnancy or breastfeeding
- Regular medication use, in particular substances affecting heart rate or glucose metabolism (e.g., beta-blockers, antiarrhythmics, antidiabetics)
- Regular cigarette smoking (> 1 cigarette per day) and/or cannabis use
- Known intolerance to the study preparations (isomaltulose, maltodextrin, fructose)
